On curves with one place at infinityThanks: The first author is partially supported by the project GDR CNRS 2945 and a GENIL-SSV 2014 grantThanks: The second author is supported by the projects MTM2010-15595, FQM-343, FQM-5849, Géanpyl (FR nº2963 du CNRS), and FEDER funds

Abdallah Assi Address: Université d’Angers, Mathématiques, 49045 Angers ceded 01, France Email address: assi@univ-angers.fr and Pedro A. García-Sánchez Address: Departamento de Álgebra, Universidad de Granada, E-18071 Granada, España Email address: pedro@ugr.es URL: www.ugr.es/local/pedro
Abstract.

Let ff be a plane curve. We give a procedure based on Abhyankar’s approximate roots to detect if it has a single place at infinity, and if so construct its associated δ\delta-sequence, and consequently its value semigroup. Also for fixed genus (equivalently Frobenius number) we construct all δ\delta-sequences generating numerical semigroups with this given genus. For a δ\delta-sequence we present a procedure to construct all curves having this associated sequence.

We also study the embeddings of such curves in the plane. In particular, we prove that polynomial curves might not have a unique embedding.

Key words and phrases: 
one place curve, semigroup of values, approximate roots
2010 Mathematics Subject Classification
14R05, 14Q05, 68W01, 20M14

Introduction

Let 𝕂{\mathbb{K}} be an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero and let f⁡(x,y)=yn+a1​(x)​yn−1+⋯+an​(x)f(x,y)=y^{n}+a_{1}(x)y^{n-1}+\dots+a_{n}(x) be a nonzero polynomial of 𝕂​[x]​[y]{\mathbb{K}}[x][y]. Assume, after possibly a change of variables, that degx⁡(ai​(x))<i\deg_{x}(a_{i}(x))<i for all 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n. Write f⁡(x,y)=yn+∑i,j,i+j<nci​j​xi​yjf(x,y)=y^{n}+\sum_{i,j,i+j<n}c_{ij}x^{i}y^{j} and let F⁡(x,y,u)=yn+∑ci​j​un−i−j​xi​yj∈𝕂⁡[u,x,y]F(x,y,u)=y^{n}+\sum c_{ij}u^{n-i-j}x^{i}y^{j}\in{\mathbb{K}}[u,x,y]. Let CC be the curve f=0f=0 in 𝕂2{\mathbb{K}}^{2}. Then the projective curve C¯:F=0\bar{C}:F=0 is the projective closure of CC in 𝐏K2{\bf P}_{K}^{2}. Furthermore, p=(0,1,0)p=(0,1,0) is the unique point at infinity of C¯\bar{C} and F⁡(u,1,y)F(u,1,y) is the local equation of C¯\bar{C} at pp. We say that ff has one place at infinity if F⁡(u,1,y)F(u,1,y) is analytically irreducible in 𝕂⁡[[u,y]]{\mathbb{K}}[[u,y]]. Curves with one place at infinity play an important role in affine geometry. In particular, it has been proved in [1] and [6] that if ff has one place at infinity, then so is for f−λf-\lambda for all λ∈𝕂\lambda\in{\mathbb{K}}. Also, we can associate with ff a numerical semigroup that has some good properties (it is free, and thus a complete intersection and symmetric). By using the arithmetic of the semigroup of a polynomial with one place at infinity and its approximate roots, S.S. Abhyankar and T.T. Moh proved that given two polynomials x⁡(t),y⁡(t)∈𝕂⁡[t]x(t),y(t)\in{\mathbb{K}}[t] with tt-degrees n>mn>m, if 𝕂⁡[x⁡(t),y⁡(t)]=𝕂⁡[t]{\mathbb{K}}[x(t),y(t)]={\mathbb{K}}[t], then mm divides nn, showing that a coordinate of 𝕂2{\mathbb{K}}^{2} has a unique embedding in 𝕂2{\mathbb{K}}^{2}.

The study of polynomials with one place at infinity is also motivated by the plane Jacobian conjecture. Let g∈𝕂⁡[x,y]g\in{\mathbb{K}}[x,y]. This conjecture says the following: if the Jacobian J⁡(f,g)J(f,g) is a nonzero constant, then 𝕂⁡[x,y]=𝕂⁡[f,g]{\mathbb{K}}[x,y]={\mathbb{K}}[f,g]. If 𝕂⁡[x,y]=𝕂⁡[f,g]{\mathbb{K}}[x,y]={\mathbb{K}}[f,g], then ff is equivalent to a coordinate, in particular ff has one place at infinity. Hence the plane Jacobian conjecture is equivalent to the following: if J⁡(f,g)J(f,g) is a nonzero constant, then ff has one place at infinity. Despite a lot of activities, this conjecture is still open.

Let ff be as above and let gg be a polynomial of 𝕂⁡[x,y]{\mathbb{K}}[x,y]. Let C1C_{1} be the affine curve g=0g=0. We say that CC is isomorphic to C1C_{1} if the ring of coordinates 𝕂⁡[C]{\mathbb{K}}[C] and 𝕂⁡[C1]{\mathbb{K}}[C_{1}] are isomorphic. We say that CC is equivalent to C1C_{1} if f=σ⁡(g)f=\sigma(g) for some automorphism σ\sigma of 𝕂⁡[x,y]{\mathbb{K}}[x,y]. It is natural to ask which isomorphic curves are equivalent. Curves with one place at infinity, with their good properties, offer a good setting where this question can be studied.

The main aim of this paper is to give an algorithmic approach to the study of curves with one place at infinity, together with an implementation in the semigroup package GAP ([11]). Our contributions in this direction are the following. For (2) and (3) we make extensive use of the concept of δ\delta-sequence (see Page 2.1).

  1. (1)

    (Section 3) Given a polynomial f∈𝕂⁡[x,y]f\in{\mathbb{K}}[x,y], decide if ff has one place at infinity and if yes, compute the set of its approximate roots and the generators of its semigroup. Our approach here is the irreducibility criterion given by S.S. Abhyankar in [4]. This criterion is straightforward from the equation. It is based on the notion of generalized Newton polygons and it does not use neither the resolution of singularities nor the calculation of Puiseux series at infinity. We have implemented this procedure using the numericalsgps ([9]) GAP ([11]) package, and named it SemigroupOfValuesOfPlaneCurveWithSinglePlaceAtInfinity.

  2. (2)

    (Section 4) Given a sequence of integers in ℕ{\mathbb{N}}, decide if this sequence generates the semigroup of a polynomial at infinity, and if it is the case, calculate an equation of such a polynomial. Our equation allows in particular, using the notion of generalized Newton polygons, the calculation of all polynomials with the given semigroup. The GAP function implemented for this is CurveAssociatedToDeltaSequence (compare with [10, Algorithm 1]).

  3. (3)

    (Section 5) Given a positive integer gg, compute the set of semigroups of polynomials with one place at infinity with genus gg (hence with conductor 2​g2g). Note that if Γ\Gamma is such a semigroup and if ff is a polynomial with one place at infinity whose semigroup is Γ\Gamma, then gg is the geometric genus of a nonsingular element of the pencil (f−λ)λ∈𝕂(f-\lambda)_{\lambda\in{\mathbb{K}}}, and 2​g2g is the rank of the 𝕂{\mathbb{K}}-vector space 𝕂⁡[x,y]/(fx,fy){{\mathbb{K}}[x,y]}/{(f_{x},f_{y})}, where fxf_{x} (respectively fyf_{y}) denotes the xx-derivative (respectively the yy-derivative) of ff. The function DeltaSequencesWithFrobeniusNumber has been designed to do this. In [10] there is an alternative procedure to compute all δ\delta-sequences with given genus.

All these GAP functions will be included in the next release of the package numericalsgps.

In Section 1 we recall the main properties of curves with one place at infinity and we give a proof of Abhyanlar-Moh Theorem: a rational nonsingular one place curve is equivalent to a coordinate of 𝕂2{\mathbb{K}}^{2}. In Section 2 we explicitly describe the automorphism that transforms the equation of the curve into a coordinate. The method of the proof allows us to give a simple demonstration of the fact that two equivalent polynomials with one place at infinity have the same δ\delta-sequences. In the last section, we study the embedding of polynomial curves (rational curves with one place at infinity). In particular, we give an example of a polynomial curve with two inequivalent embeddings in the affine plane.

1. Semigroup of one place at infinity curves

Let f⁡(x,y)=yn+a1​(x)​yn−1+⋯+an​(x)f(x,y)=y^{n}+a_{1}(x)y^{n-1}+\dots+a_{n}(x) be a nonzero polynomial of 𝕂​[x]​[y]{\mathbb{K}}[x][y] and assume, after possibly a change of variables, that for all 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n, degx⁡ai​(x)<i\deg_{x}a_{i}(x)<i. Assume that ff has one place at infinity. Given a polynomial g∈𝕂⁡[x,y]g\in{\mathbb{K}}[x,y], we define the intersection of ff with gg, denoted int(f,g)(f,g), to be the rank of the 𝕂{\mathbb{K}}-vector space 𝕂⁡[x,y]/(f,g){{{\mathbb{K}}[x,y]}/{(f,g)}}. Clearly 0=int⁡(f,1)0=\mathrm{int}(f,1) and int(f,g1​g2)=int⁡(f,g1)+int⁡(f,g2)(f,g_{1}g_{2})=\mathrm{int}(f,g_{1})+\mathrm{int}(f,g_{2}).

The set {int⁡(f,g)∣g∈𝕂⁡[x,y]∖(f)}\{\mathrm{int}(f,g)\mid g\in{\mathbb{K}}[x,y]\setminus(f)\} is a subsemigroup of ℕ{\mathbb{N}}. We denote it by Γ⁡(f)\Gamma(f), and we say that Γ⁡(f)\Gamma(f) is the Abhyankar semigroup associated to ff. We also say that a subsemigroup Γ\Gamma of ℕ\mathbb{N} is an Abhyankar semigroup if there exists ff such that Γ=Γ⁡(f)\Gamma=\Gamma(f) (for basic properties on numerical semigroups, please, refer to [12]).

Assume, after possibly a change of variables, that a1​(x)=0a_{1}(x)=0. In particular Appn​(f)=y\mathrm{App}_{n}(f)=y. For all k≥2k\geq 2, let dk=gcd⁡(dk−1,rk−1)d_{k}=\gcd(d_{k-1},r_{k-1}), gk=Appdk​(f)g_{k}=\mathrm{App}_{d_{k}}(f) and rk=int⁡(f,gk)r_{k}=\mathrm{int}(f,g_{k}). 2. Reduced forms of one place curves

Let f=yn+a2​(x)​yn−2+⋯+an​(x)f=y^{n}+a_{2}(x)y^{n-2}+\dots+a_{n}(x) be a polynomial with one place at infinity and assume that n>m=degx⁡an​(x)n>m=\deg_{x}a_{n}(x). In particular this implies that degx⁡ai​(x)<i\deg_{x}a_{i}(x)<i for all i∈{1,…,n}i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}, because otherwise the Newton polygon associated to ff would have more than one edge, and consequently ff would have more than one place at infinity (see [2, Chapter 4]).

Let r¯=(r0,…,rh),d¯=(d1,…,dh,dh+1=1),e¯=(e1,…,eh)\underline{r}=(r_{0},\dots,r_{h}),\underline{d}=(d_{1},\dots,d_{h},d_{h+1}=1),\underline{e}=(e_{1},\dots,e_{h}) be the set of characteristic sequences associated with ff as in Section 1, and let g1=y,g2,…,gh,gh+1=fg_{1}=y,g_{2},\dots,g_{h},g_{h+1}=f be the set of approximate roots of ff.

Remark 8 (Generalized Newton polygons, see [4]).

Let 1≤k≤h1\leq k\leq h and let gk+1=gkek+α2​(x,y)​gkek−2+⋯+αek​(x,y)g_{k+1}=g_{k}^{e_{k}}+\alpha_{2}(x,y)g_{k}^{e_{k}-2}+\dots+\alpha_{e_{k}}(x,y) be the expansion of gk+1g_{k+1} with respect to gkg_{k}. We have the following:

  1. (i)

Example 16.

Let us compute a curve associated to the δ\delta-sequence (6,4,3)(6,4,3). In order to see the recursive process, we set the information level of the numericalsgps package to 2.

gap> SetInfoLevel(InfoNumSgps,2);
gap> CurveAssociatedToDeltaSequence([6,4,3]);
#I  Temporal curve: y^3-x^2
#I  Temporal curve: y^6-2*x^2*y^3+x^4-x
y^6-2*x^2*y^3+x^4-x

5. Abhyankar semigroups with a given genus

Let gg be a positive integer and let μ=2​g\mu=2g. There exists a numerical symmetric semigroup Γ\Gamma and a system of generators of Γ\Gamma such that the following conditions hold:

  1. (1)

    μ\mu is the conductor C⁡(Γ)\mathrm{C}(\Gamma) of Γ\Gamma,

  2. (2)

    Γ=⟨r0,r1,…,rh⟩\Gamma=\langle r_{0},r_{1},\dots,r_{h}\rangle, r0>r1r_{0}>r_{1}, and (r0,…,r1)(r_{0},\dots,r_{1}) is a δ\delta-sequence.

In particular, Γ=Γ⁡(f)\Gamma=\Gamma(f), where f∈𝕂⁡[x,y]f\in{\mathbb{K}}[x,y] is a polynomial with one place at infinity such that rdeg⁡(f)=r0\mathrm{rdeg}(f)=r_{0}. The simplest example of such a semigroup if ⟨μ+1,2⟩\langle\mu+1,2\rangle. Note that if Γ\Gamma is such a semigroup, then μ≥2​(2h−1)\mu\geq 2(2^{h}-1) (see [7, Proposition 6.7]). In particular h≤b=log2⁡(g+1)h\leq b=\log_{2}(g+1). Let 1≤h≤b1\leq h\leq b.

In light of Proposition 4, if we denote by μh=C⁡(⟨r0/dh,…,rh−1/dh⟩)\mu_{h}=\mathrm{C}(\langle r_{0}/d_{h},\ldots,r_{h-1}/d_{h}\rangle), then μ=dh​μh+(dh−1)​rh−dh+1=dh​μh+(rh−1)​(dh−1)\mu=d_{h}\mu_{h}+(d_{h}-1)r_{h}-d_{h}+1=d_{h}\mu_{h}+(r_{h}-1)(d_{h}-1) and gcd⁡(rh,dh)=dh+1=1\gcd(r_{h},d_{h})=d_{h+1}=1.

  • •

    If h=1h=1, then μ=(r0−1)​(r1−1)\mu=(r_{0}-1)(r_{1}-1). Since r0>r1r_{0}>r_{1}, (r1−1)2<μ(r_{1}-1)^{2}<\mu. Hence r1<μ+1r_{1}<\sqrt{\mu}+1, which is less than or equal to μ−1\mu-1 for all μ≥4\mu\geq 4. Notice that μ\mu cannot be 33, and the case μ=2\mu=2 is ⟨3,2⟩\langle 3,2\rangle.

  • •

    For h>1h>1, dh​μh>1d_{h}\mu_{h}>1 and dh≥2d_{h}\geq 2. Consequently, rh−1≤(rh−1)​(dh−1)=μ−dh​μh<μ−1r_{h}-1\leq(r_{h}-1)(d_{h}-1)=\mu-d_{h}\mu_{h}<\mu-1, whence rh<μr_{h}<\mu.

Observe also that μ−1\mu-1 is the Frobenius number of Γ\Gamma, and so rh≠μ−1r_{h}\neq\mu-1. This implies that for Γ≠⟨3,2⟩\Gamma\neq\langle 3,2\rangle,

2≤rh≤μ−2.2\leq r_{h}\leq\mu-2.

Thus there are finitely many possible rhr_{h}, and for each of these rhr_{h}, (dh−1)​(rh−1)≤(dh−1)​(rh−1)+dh​μh=μ(d_{h}-1)(r_{h}-1)\leq(d_{h}-1)(r_{h}-1)+d_{h}\mu_{h}=\mu. Hence

2≤dh≤μrh−1+1.2\leq d_{h}\leq\frac{\mu}{r_{h}-1}+1.

For each pair rhr_{h} and dhd_{h} we find recursively the sequences ⟨r0′,…,rh−1′⟩\langle r_{0}^{\prime},\ldots,r_{h-1}^{\prime}\rangle with conductor μh\mu_{h}. This was the idea used to implement DeltaSequencesWithFrobeniusNumber.

Remark 17.

From Lemma 3, int⁡(f,fy)=μ+r0−1≤r0​(r0−1)\mathrm{int}(f,f_{y})=\mu+r_{0}-1\leq r_{0}(r_{0}-1) by Bézout’s Theorem. Hence μ≤(r0−1)2\mu\leq(r_{0}-1)^{2}, which implies that r0≥μ+1r_{0}\geq\sqrt{\mu}+1.

Example 18.

It may happen that several δ\delta-sequences generate the same numerical semigroup. This is why in general there are more δ\delta-sequences than Abhyankar semigroups for a fixed genus.

gap> l:=DeltaSequencesWithFrobeniusNumber(13);
[ [ 6, 4, 11 ], [ 8, 3 ], [ 8, 6, 3 ], [ 9, 6, 5 ], [ 10, 4, 7 ], [ 12, 8, 3 ],
  [ 12, 8, 6, 3 ], [ 15, 2 ], [ 15, 6, 2 ], [ 15, 10, 2 ] ]
gap> Length(l);
10
gap> Length(Set(l,NumericalSemigroup));
5

Next figure plots the number of Abhyankar semigroups and δ\delta-sequences.

The following plotting compares the number of Abhyankar semigroups with given genus with other well known families of complete intersection numerical semigroups.

Let Γ\Gamma be a semigroup with conductor μ=2​g\mu=2g and let ff be a polynomial with one place at infinity such that Γ⁡(f)=Γ\Gamma(f)=\Gamma. Let (f−λ)λ∈𝕂(f-\lambda)_{\lambda\in{\mathbb{K}}} be the pencil of polynomials defined by ff. Given an element F=f−λ0F=f-\lambda_{0} of the pencil, if μ∞\mu_{\infty} denotes the local Milnor number of FF at the point at infinity, then we have μ+μ∞=(r0−1)​(r0−2)\mu+\mu_{\infty}=(r_{0}-1)(r_{0}-2). Also, if gg denotes the genus of the curve V⁡(F)\mathrm{V}(F), then 2​g+∑p∈V⁡(F)μp+rp−1+μ∞=(r0−1)​(r0−2)2g+\sum_{p\in\mathrm{V}(F)}\mu_{p}+r_{p}-1+\mu_{\infty}=(r_{0}-1)(r_{0}-2), where μp\mu_{p} (respectively rpr_{p}) denotes the Milnor number (respectively the number of places) at pp. If the curve V⁡(F)\mathrm{V}(F) is nonsingular in 𝕂2{\mathbb{K}}^{2}, then 2​g+μ∞=(r0−1)​(r0−2)=μ+μ∞2g+\mu_{\infty}=(r_{0}-1)(r_{0}-2)=\mu+\mu_{\infty}, hence μ=2​g\mu=2g. In particular gg is the geometric genus of a nonsingular element of the pencil (f−λ)λ∈𝕂(f-\lambda)_{\lambda\in{\mathbb{K}}}.

6. Embedding of one place curves in the affine plane

Let f⁡(x,y)f(x,y) be a nonzero polynomial of 𝕂⁡[x,y]{\mathbb{K}}[x,y] and let A⁡(f)=𝕂⁡[x,y]/(f)A(f)={{{\mathbb{K}}[x,y]}/{(f)}}. Given another polynomial gg, we say that ff and gg are isomorphic if the two 𝕂{\mathbb{K}}-algebras A⁡(f)A(f) and A⁡(g)A(g) are isomorphic. We say that ff is equivalent to gg if g=σ⁡(f)g=\sigma(f) for some automorphism σ\sigma of 𝕂⁡[x,y]{\mathbb{K}}[x,y]. Then the following natural question arises: which isomorphic polynomials are equivalent?

Suppose that ff has one place at infinity and let gg be a polynomial with one place at infinity. It follows from Theorem 14 that if ff is equivalent to gg, then ff and gg have the same δ\delta-sequence. The converse being not true in general.

Let x⁡(t)=tn+c1​tn−1+⋯+cn,y⁡(t)=tm+c1′​tm−1+⋯+cm′x(t)=t^{n}+c_{1}t^{n-1}+\dots+c_{n},y(t)=t^{m}+c^{\prime}_{1}t^{m-1}+\dots+c^{\prime}_{m} be two polynomials of 𝕂⁡[t]{\mathbb{K}}[t]. Suppose that n>m>gcd⁡(n,m)n>m>\gcd(n,m) and let f⁡(x,y)=yn+a1​(x)​yn−1+⋯+an​(x)f(x,y)=y^{n}+a_{1}(x)y^{n-1}+\dots+a_{n}(x) be the yy-monic generator of the kernel of the map ϕ:𝕂⁡[x,y]→𝕂⁡[t],ϕ⁡(x)=x⁡(t)\phi:{\mathbb{K}}[x,y]\to{\mathbb{K}}[t],\phi(x)=x(t) and ϕ⁡(y)=y⁡(t)\phi(y)=y(t) (there is such a generator because the curve has a single place at infinity). Then ff has one place at infinity and A⁡(f)≅𝕂⁡[x⁡(t),y⁡(t)]A(f)\cong{\mathbb{K}}[x(t),y(t)]. Let gg be another curve with one place at infinity. Then ff is isomorphic to gg if and only if A(g)≅𝕂[x1(t),y1(t))]≅𝕂[x(t),y(t)]A(g)\cong{\mathbb{K}}[x_{1}(t),y_{1}(t))]\cong{\mathbb{K}}[x(t),y(t)]. We have the following result.

Proposition 19.

Let x⁡(t),y⁡(t),x1​(t),y1​(t)∈𝕂⁡[t]x(t),y(t),x_{1}(t),y_{1}(t)\in{\mathbb{K}}[t] and let ff (respectively gg) be the yy-monic generator of the map ϕ:𝕂⁡[x,y]→𝕂⁡[t],ϕ⁡(x)=x⁡(t)\phi:{\mathbb{K}}[x,y]\to{\mathbb{K}}[t],\phi(x)=x(t) and ϕ⁡(y)=y⁡(t)\phi(y)=y(t) (respectively ψ:𝕂⁡[x,y]→𝕂⁡[t],ψ⁡(x)=x1​(t),ψ⁡(y)=y1​(t)\psi:{\mathbb{K}}[x,y]\to{\mathbb{K}}[t],\psi(x)=x_{1}(t),\psi(y)=y_{1}(t)). If A⁡(f)≅𝕂⁡[x⁡(t),y⁡(t)]≅A⁡(g)≅𝕂⁡[x1​(t),y1​(t)]A(f)\cong{\mathbb{K}}[x(t),y(t)]\cong A(g)\cong{\mathbb{K}}[x_{1}(t),y_{1}(t)], then Γ⁡(f)=Γ⁡(g)\Gamma(f)=\Gamma(g).

Proof.

The fact that x⁡(t),y⁡(t)∈𝕂⁡[x1​(t),y1​(t)]x(t),y(t)\in{\mathbb{K}}[x_{1}(t),y_{1}(t)] implies that there exist P⁡(x,y),Q⁡(x,y)P(x,y),Q(x,y) such that x⁡(t)=P⁡(x1​(t),y1​(t))x(t)=P(x_{1}(t),y_{1}(t)) and y⁡(t)=Q⁡(x1​(t),y1​(t))y(t)=Q(x_{1}(t),y_{1}(t)). Let a∈Γ⁡(f)a\in\Gamma(f) and let h∈𝕂⁡[x,y]h\in{\mathbb{K}}[x,y] be such that int⁡(f,h)=degt⁡h⁡(x⁡(t),y⁡(t))=a\mathrm{int}(f,h)=\deg_{t}h(x(t),y(t))=a. If h1​(x,y)=h⁡(P⁡(x,y),Q⁡(x,y))h_{1}(x,y)=h(P(x,y),Q(x,y)), then

h1​(x1​(t),y1​(t))=h⁡(P⁡(x1​(t),y1​(t)),Q⁡(x1​(t),y1​(t))=h⁡(x⁡(t),y⁡(t))CLOSEh_{1}(x_{1}(t),y_{1}(t))=h(P(x_{1}(t),y_{1}(t)),Q(x_{1}(t),y_{1}(t))=h(x(t),y(t))

and degt⁡h1​(x1​(t),y1​(t))=a=int⁡(g,h1)\deg_{t}h_{1}(x_{1}(t),y_{1}(t))=a=\mathrm{int}(g,h_{1}), whence a∈Γ⁡(g)a\in\Gamma(g). We prove in a similar way that Γ⁡(g)\Gamma(g) is contained in Γ⁡(f)\Gamma(f). ∎

Example 20.

Isomorphic does not imply equivalent for polynomial curves. Let z⁡(t)=t3−a,a≠0,x⁡(t)=t​z​(t)=t4−a​tz(t)=t^{3}-a,a\not=0,x(t)=tz(t)=t^{4}-at, and y⁡(t)=z​(t)2+a2​z​(t)y(t)=z(t)^{2}+\frac{a}{2}z(t). We have x​(t)3=t3​z​(t)3=z​(t)4+a​z​(t)3x(t)^{3}=t^{3}z(t)^{3}=z(t)^{4}+az(t)^{3}. We shall prove that 𝕂⁡[x⁡(t),y⁡(t)]=𝕂⁡[x⁡(t),z⁡(t)]{\mathbb{K}}[x(t),y(t)]={\mathbb{K}}[x(t),z(t)]. The first inclusion is clear. Also, y​(t)2=z​(t)4+a​z​(t)2+a24​z​(t)2=x​(t)3+a24​y​(t)−a38​z​(t)y(t)^{2}=z(t)^{4}+az(t)^{2}+\frac{a^{2}}{4}z(t)^{2}=x(t)^{3}+\frac{a^{2}}{4}y(t)-\frac{a^{3}}{8}z(t), whence a38​z​(t)=y​(t)2−x​(t)3−a24​y​(t)∈𝕂⁡[x⁡(t),y⁡(t)]\frac{a^{3}}{8}z(t)=y(t)^{2}-x(t)^{3}-\frac{a^{2}}{4}y(t)\in{\mathbb{K}}[x(t),y(t)]. Let ff (respectively gg) be the yy-monic generator of the map ϕ:𝕂⁡[x,y]→𝕂⁡[t]\phi:{\mathbb{K}}[x,y]\to{\mathbb{K}}[t], ϕ⁡(x)=x⁡(t)\phi(x)=x(t) and ϕ⁡(y)=y⁡(t)\phi(y)=y(t) (respectively ψ:𝕂⁡[x,y]→𝕂⁡[t]\psi:{\mathbb{K}}[x,y]\to{\mathbb{K}}[t], ψ⁡(x)=x⁡(t)\psi(x)=x(t), ψ⁡(y)=z⁡(t)\psi(y)=z(t)). Then f⁡(x,y)=12​a2​x3​y−12​a2​y3+x6−2​x3​y2+y4+116​a4​x3=(y3−x2−14​a2)2+12​a2​x3​y+116​a4​x3−12​a2​x2−116​a4f(x,y)=\frac{1}{2}a^{2}x^{3}y-\frac{1}{2}a^{2}y^{3}+x^{6}-2x^{3}y^{2}+y^{4}+\frac{1}{16}a^{4}x^{3}=\left(y^{3}-x^{2}-\frac{1}{4}a^{2}\right)^{2}+\frac{1}{2}a^{2}x^{3}y+\frac{1}{16}a^{4}x^{3}-\frac{1}{2}a^{2}x^{2}-\frac{1}{16}a^{4} and g⁡(x,y)=y4+a​y3−x3g(x,y)=y^{4}+ay^{3}-x^{3}. Hence the δ\delta-sequence of ff (resp. gg) is ⟨6,4,3⟩\langle 6,4,3\rangle (resp. ⟨4,3⟩\langle 4,3\rangle). By Theorem 14, ff is not equivalent to gg.

This example provides a counter example for the conjecture stated in [13].

Remark 21.
  1. (i)

    Let f⁡(x,y)=1−x​yf(x,y)=1-xy and g⁡(x,y)=1−x​yk,k≥2g(x,y)=1-xy^{k},k\geq 2. Let C1:f=0C_{1}:f=0, Ck:g=0C_{k}:g=0, and let ϕ:C1→Ck,ϕ⁡(a,b)=(ak,b)\phi:C_{1}\to C_{k},\phi(a,b)=(a^{k},b) and ψ:Ck→C1,ψ⁡(c,d)=(c​dk−1,d)\psi:C_{k}\to C_{1},\psi(c,d)=(cd^{k-1},d). We have ψ∘ϕ⁡(a,b)=ψ⁡(ak,b)=(ak​bk−1,b)=((a​b)k−1​a,b)=(a,b)\psi\circ\phi(a,b)=\psi(a^{k},b)=(a^{k}b^{k-1},b)=((ab)^{k-1}a,b)=(a,b) and ϕ∘ψ⁡(c,d)=ϕ⁡(c​dk−1,d)=(ck​dk⁡(k−1),d)=(c​(c​dk)k−1,d)=(c,d)\phi\circ\psi(c,d)=\phi(cd^{k-1},d)=(c^{k}d^{k(k-1)},d)=(c(cd^{k})^{k-1},d)=(c,d). Hence C1C_{1} and CkC_{k} are isomorphic. Clearly C1C_{1} and CkC_{k} are not equivalent. Thus we have infinitely many inequivalent embeddings of C1C_{1} in the affine plane. Note that C1C_{1} (respectively CkC_{k}) has two places at infinity.

  2. (ii)

    Let f⁡(x,y)f(x,y) be a plane curve with one place at infinity and let r⁡(f)=yn+a2​(x)​yn−2+⋯+an​(x)\mathrm{r}(f)=y^{n}+a_{2}(x)y^{n-2}+\dots+a_{n}(x). If gg is another one place curve such that A⁡(f)A(f) is isomorphic to A⁡(g)A(g), then Γ⁡(f)=Γ⁡(g)\Gamma(f)=\Gamma(g). Hence the number of nonequivalent embeddings of ff is bounded by the number of semigroups Γ¯=⟨r0,r1,…,rh⟩\bar{\Gamma}=\langle r_{0},r_{1},\dots,r_{h}\rangle such that:

    1. (1)

      Γ¯=Γ⁡(f)\bar{\Gamma}=\Gamma(f),

    2. (2)

      Γ¯=⟨r0,r1,…,rh⟩\bar{\Gamma}=\langle r_{0},r_{1},\dots,r_{h}\rangle and (r0,r1,…,rh)(r_{0},r_{1},\dots,r_{h}) is a δ\delta-sequence.

Example 22.

Let f⁡(x,y)f(x,y) be such that Γ⁡(f)=⟨7,6⟩\Gamma(f)=\langle 7,6\rangle. We have μ⁡(f)=30\mu(f)=30. Let h=2h=2 and let Γ¯=⟨r0,r1,r2⟩\bar{\Gamma}=\langle r_{0},r_{1},r_{2}\rangle with the Properties (1) and (2). Since 77 is a prime number, r0>7r_{0}>7. Hence r0∈⟨7,6⟩r_{0}\in\langle 7,6\rangle. Furthermore, r2r_{2} is either 66 or 77. If r2=6r_{2}=6, then d2=7d_{2}=7. Thus μ⁡(f)=30=μ2​d2+(d2−1)​(r2−1)=7​μ2+30\mu(f)=30=\mu_{2}d_{2}+(d_{2}-1)(r_{2}-1)=7\mu_{2}+30, and μ2=0\mu_{2}=0. In particular (r0,7,6)(r_{0},7,6) is not reduced. Finally r2=7r_{2}=7 and d2=2,3d_{2}=2,3. This gives us the following solutions: δ1=(14,6,7)\delta_{1}=(14,6,7), and δ2=(21,6,7)\delta_{2}=(21,6,7). Note that if f⁡(x,y)=y7−x6−xf(x,y)=y^{7}-x^{6}-x, g⁡(x,y)=(y7−x3)2−xg(x,y)=(y^{7}-x^{3})^{2}-x, h⁡(x,y)=(y7−x2)3−xh(x,y)=(y^{7}-x^{2})^{3}-x, then A⁡(f),A⁡(g)A(f),A(g), and A⁡(h)A(h) are isomorphic (though they are not equivalent since their associated δ\delta-sequences are different).

We can perform this task with our GAP implementation.

gap> s:=NumericalSemigroup(6,7);
<Modular numerical semigroup satisfying 7x mod 42 <= x >
gap> FrobeniusNumber(s);
29
gap> DeltaSequencesWithFrobeniusNumber(29);
[ [ 7, 6 ], [ 8, 6, 19 ], [ 9, 6, 13 ], [ 10, 6, 15 ], [ 11, 4 ], [ 12, 8, 10, 15 ],
  [ 12, 8, 14, 11 ], [ 12, 9, 7 ], [ 14, 4, 19 ], [ 14, 6, 7 ], [ 15, 6, 10 ],
  [ 15, 10, 6 ], [ 16, 3 ], [ 16, 6, 3 ], [ 16, 12, 3 ],  [ 16, 12, 6, 3 ],
  [ 18, 4, 15 ], [ 18, 12, 9, 7 ],[ 18, 12, 15, 4 ], [ 21, 6, 7 ], [ 22, 4, 11 ],
  [ 24, 16, 3 ], [ 24, 16, 6, 3 ], [ 24, 16, 12, 3 ],  [ 24, 16, 12, 6, 3 ],
  [ 27, 6, 4 ], [ 31, 2 ] ]
gap> Filtered(last, gs->NumericalSemigroup(gs)=s);
[ [ 7, 6 ], [ 14, 6, 7 ], [ 21, 6, 7 ] ]

In general, given ff, this procedure gives us the δ\delta-sequences of the candidates gg such that A⁡(f)≅A⁡(g)A(f)\cong A(g).
